questions.question: An orchestrator is planning their workflow for a session. Should they write implementation code directly in the main session or delegate execution to subagents?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Delegate the implementation to subagents; keep the main session for planning and integration.** That's the standard guidance in the Claude Code subagents docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents, section "Choose between subagents and main conversation", which I fetched and read):

**Keep it in the main session when:**
- the work needs frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement
- multiple phases share significant context (planning → implementation → testing)
- it's a quick, targeted change
- latency matters — a fresh (non-fork) subagent starts with no conversation history and spends time re-gathering context

**Delegate to subagents when:**
- the task produces verbose output you won't reference again (test-suite output, logs, file dumps) — the subagent burns its own context and only a summary returns to the main session
- the work is self-contained and can return a summary
- you want to enforce tool restrictions/permissions on the worker
- the work is independent and can run in parallel

So the shape of a well-planned session is: the main session holds the plan, dispatches self-contained implementation chunks (each with a clear task description), receives summaries, integrates the results, and does the review. questions.question: The orchestrator notices context usage is around 50%, with several pending tasks left in the queue. Is it appropriate to wrap up the session early?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No — at ~50% context, the orchestrator should keep working, not wrap up.** Pending tasks in the queue are the opposite of a stop condition: an idle fleet is a trigger to **dispatch**, and 50% is well under every gate in the operating rules.

The rule (`operating-memory/workflow/do-not-wind-down-early.md` in `sini/genie-agent`, main) sets context-budget gates:

| context reading | gate |
| --- | --- |
| **< 75%** | start new work freely — new subjects, sweeps, lanes |
| >= 75% | no fresh **subjects**; finish every open stream (fix rounds, gate contacts, landings, banking, filing) |
| >= 90% | close out: bank obligations into tracker bodies, write the handoff |
| weekly quota >= 95% | clean, unhurried closeout (evaluated last, outranks context gates, restricts only new dispatch) |

So at ~50% the correct move is to drain the queue — dispatch the pending tasks — and only at 75% stop starting *new subjects* (delivery of underway work continues), with closeout reserved for 90%+.

The rule exists because this exact situation was measured and cost the owner attention:

- One session closed six rows, published them, summarised and **stopped at 54% context**; the owner had to prod it back to work.
- In another, four self-estimates read ~76/81/85/88% against real readings of 48% and 59% — every estimate high, each acted on by declining to dispatch.

The rule's logic: an **early stop throws away the session's remaining capacity and cannot be recovered**; a late stop is recoverable (compaction, then re-boot from the resume prompt and handoff). It also warns that drafting a handoff early (say, at 54%) is wasted work — the handoff file is wholesale-replaced at close, so it would just be rewritten at 90%. Act only on a real context reading, never an estimate; if unknown, say "unknown, last reading N%" and keep working.

One caveat: this rule is marked `scope: local` with owner-set values (2026-09-12) — it encodes this setup's choices, so a downstream orchestrator should rethink the 75/90/95 thresholds before adopting them. (And note this is the orchestrator/multi-agent rule; genie's per-thread *support* sessions have a separate lifecycle — destroyed after acceptance or 24h idle, per design ruling 8 — where context % is not the end condition at all.)

How I know: I read the rule from `sini/genie-agent` main — the `operating-memory/MEMORY.md` index line ("Do not wind down early — false stop conditions") and the file itself (rule, measured why, the gate table, false stop conditions).

questions.question: When working in a shared git checkout where another peer agent is actively modifying files, how should changes be committed?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"In a shared checkout, commit **only your own files, by explicit path** — never sweep the whole working tree.

1. **Stage only your files:** `git add <your-file-1> <your-file-2> ...`. Avoid `git add -A` and `git commit -a`: the peer agent's half-written or in-flight files are in the same working tree, and a tree-wide stage would commit their work under your commit message (and their work would be lost from their hands).
2. **Commit as normal.** Your commit lands on top of whatever HEAD is at that moment — including commits your peer agent has already made.
3. **Rebase before pushing:** `git fetch && git rebase` (or `git pull --rebase`) so your commit stacks on the peer agent's new commits instead of forking the branch and leaving someone to resolve the divergence.
4. **Leave the peer agent's uncommitted files untouched:** don't stash, checkout, or revert them; if you must move them out of the way, that's a conversation, not a silent `git stash`.
5. **If the two of you keep colliding, isolate with a worktree:** `git worktree add ../<name> <branch>` gives each agent its own working tree and branch on the same repo — the cleanest fix, and no shared working tree to contend over at all.

Caveat: I could not reach the operating-memory mount and `recall` had no recorded answer for this practice, so this is stated from general git working-tree practice rather than a verified team record.","confidence":0.5,"gaps":["Could not verify the team's recorded practice: recall (memory and support banks) returned no matching entry and the /memory mount was not accessible from this thread"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: What is the default review stance for an adversarial gate reviewer evaluating a submitted patch or spec?
When dispatched as a scout to measure an issue across repositories, should the scout fix small bugs found during measurement?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"No — a scout measures, it does not fix. A scout dispatched to measure an issue across repositories should report small bugs it finds, not fix them, and the fixing should go out as a separate dispatch (or to the agent that owns the issue).

Three reasons, all grounded in conventions that are visible in the ecosystem's own docs:

1. **A fix changes what you are measuring.** The scout's output is a measurement of the current state, per repository. Patching a bug mid-scan changes the state the later measurements are taken against, so the results stop describing the issue as it was and stop being comparable across repos. Measurement integrity is the whole point of the dispatch.

2. **One job per role is the design rule here.** gen's core discipline is "each library owns exactly one concern" (stated in the gen hub README), and den's code style rule is "Minimal changes: fix the bug, don't refactor surroundings." A scout that starts fixing has blended two roles: the report stops being a report and the fix is made without the fixer's full context (ownership of the issue, its tests, its review gate).

3. **A "small" fix is not cheap.** Under den's conventions a fix means a failing test first, formatting, and CI validation — that is the fixer's workflow, with its own time and state changes, and doing it inside a measurement run risks scope creep across several repositories at once.

What the scout *should* do with a bug it finds: record it in the measurement report with evidence (repo, file, line, how it interferes with the measurement), and work around it read-only if it sits in the measurement path. If the bug makes the measurement impossible, the scout reports "could not measure: because of X" and hands back, rather than fixing X and silently changing the result.

How I know, and what I could not verify: I searched both recall banks (no scout entries) and ran a source-wide search across all public `sini` and `denful` repositories — the term "scout" appears in none of them, so the scout's actual charter is in private material I could not read (the gen-harness README references `den-ag-design`, which is not public). questions.question: If a harness default instruction conflicts with local project directives or design records, which one governs?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The local project directives and the design records govern; the harness's defaults are the baseline the project can override. Concretely, in the gen-harness ecosystem:

1. **The project's declaration beats the harness's default.** The harness's default is that a repo's root `AGENTS.md` is a capability *sheet* (`gen.ci.agentsMd.sheet = "owed"`, the default of `lib.checks.agentsMdCitations`). A consumer whose `AGENTS.md` is agent *instructions* declares `sheet = "instructions"`, and one that owes no sheet declares `"not-owed"` — the check then requires the file to exist non-empty and reads no citation region from it. "There is no fourth value and no silent arm: a declaration the tree contradicts is refused in every direction." So when the project's local directive conflicts with what the harness assumes by default, the project's declared role wins, and the check only verifies that the declaration and the tree agree.

2. **The harness never adjudicates truth.** `agents-md-citations.nix` states it in its own failure message: "This check reads whether the evidence a claim offers still EXISTS, never whether the claim is true." The AGENTS.md capability sheet likewise says of the harness: "Deciding whether a documentation claim is TRUE — nobody here." The harness gates citations and structure; the content belongs to the project. gen-harness's own root `CLAUDE.md` models this: it defers to the repo's `AGENTS.md` ("Read it on demand: before changing this library's exports…"), rather than carrying the sheet's content itself.

3. **The design record is the reference, above both.** The published capability reference for each library lives in the design repo (`den-ag-design`, under `gen-specs/<lib>/REFERENCE.md`); the in-repo sheet "is the in-repo half and is not that document." The operating memory states the precedence for defaults explicitly: a default "does NOT extend to designs," the same "goes for defaults that refine an owner ruling," and "the rule that a new thing's spec waits for an approved design is more specific and outranks" the general default rule; M-tier work is "fully determined by an existing ruling or spec." So: an approved design record / owner ruling outranks a harness default, and local directives outrank the harness's default assumptions.

4. **If two absolute rules genuinely collide and no ruling covers the pair, no default silently resolves it.** The `rule-conflicts` practice: "There is no general precedence order between rules." A wording conflict is fixed by rewording; a genuine trade-off gets a row in `practices/rule-conflicts.md`; a pair not in the table "goes to the owner as a D-tier question, and the ruling becomes a new row."

How I know: I read `sini/gen-harness` on `main` — `CLAUDE.md` (defers to the repo's `AGENTS.md`), `AGENTS.md` (the "Not this repository's job" table: nobody in the harness decides claim truth; the published reference is den-ag-design's, the sheet is its in-repo half), `README.md` (the `sheet = "not-owed" | "instructions"` declarations), and `agents-md-citations.nix` (the `sheet ? Caveat: `den-ag-design` is a private repo (404 to me), so if it carries an explicit ruling phrased exactly as "harness default vs local directive," I have not read it — the answer above is composed from the sources I could verify, which all point the same way.","confidence":0.75,"gaps":["den-ag-design (the design repo holding gen-specs/<lib>/REFERENCE.md) is private and returned 404; did not read any ruling there that phrases this precedence explicitly","Interpreted 'harness' as gen-harness (the CI harness); if the asker means the xmsg svc:/herdr agent harness's default session instructions, that specific conflict rule was not verified","No prior answer in the support bank matched this question (recall returned nothing)"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: What should an orchestrator do if multiple subagents complete their dispatches and sit idle while context remains low?
What essential elements must be provided when writing a dispatch brief for a leaf agent?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"In the genie-agent operating memory, a **leaf agent** is a dispatched subagent — one of the four roles `scout | spec | gate | build`, who "do not dispatch their own agents". The division of labour is the key idea: the agent carries the **standing half** (instrument facts, measurement law, reporting and hand-off protocol — `roles/common-protocol.md`), and the **brief carries the task half, and links rather than restates** (`workflow/dispatch-form.md`). So a dispatch brief must provide these essential elements:

**1. Identity and routing**
- `You are <task-id>-<role>` (name every agent; the roster shows it) and `Agent: scout | spec | gate | build`
- `CARRIER: <tracker id>` — the place findings return
- `CLAIM:` mark the tracker item `in_progress` **before** sending; release at return (an unclaimed item with an agent on it is "a tracker that lies")
- `TIER: M | D | R`

**2. What lands and what authorizes it**
- `TARGET:` the component this lands **and** the demo/corpus example (gen-demo for gen) that exercises it — same landing; a component with no exercising example is not landed
- `DESIGN:` pointer to the owner-approved design, or "existing component". *A brief naming a NEW component without one is not dispatchable*
- `SIZING:` lands in one dispatch with its integration arm green, or split before sending

**3. Premises — tagged, conclusions only**
- Every premise line tagged: `[MEASURED <sha>]` with the re-runnable command, `[RELAYED <source>]` with who said it, or `[ASSUMED]`. A tracker-body citation is `[RELAYED]`, not `[MEASURED]` (the command proves the artefact *says* this, not that it's *true*). Measured: a brief carried a false load-bearing claim in 4/8, 4/8, 5/8, 8/8 of sampled runs
- Quote the measured **row**, not the generalising sentence (distrust "uniformly", "only", ratios, "already verified"); tag per clause; open the target before writing a premise; cite path + clause + revision
- Write "re-derive, do not copy" and give permission to falsify ("if any of this is false against the tree, that is a finding I want; do not work around it")

**4. Scope**
- `IN:` exactly what to touch
- `OUT:` what is excluded, and why it is not an oversight
- `CLASS:` instance | discharge the class (and how to enumerate members) — the trigger to discharge the class is the *second* member found

**5. Deliverables and write authority**
- A **disk path for every deliverable** (`reports/<task-id>-<subject>-<role>-v0.md`; check the path is free first). Measured: 6/8 agents finished correct work and went idle silently; every deliverable named by path was recovered, the one named only "report X" was lost
- The `WRITE | COMMIT | COMMIT+PUSH` verb, **per repo**; fence a repo only where a competing writer exists
- `WORKTREE: <path> at <explicit sha>` (one writer per worktree) or shared checkout pinned to a sha
- Standing safety clauses: never use pkill/killall or kill pgrep -f output; a memory cap for heavy evaluation; population by membership; anchors as binding names, not line numbers

**6. Oracle and exit**
- The **property** to satisfy, the **oracle** (its RED and GREEN, evaluated before the cell is written and stated in the brief), and what a **failing** run looks like
- `EXIT:` the gating oracle (component landed, consumer builds, example green) and **who confirms it** — if you cannot state EXIT, you do not yet know what you are asking for
- FAIL-IF conditions that tell a live claim from a quoted refuted one
- The mechanism rule: *"a better mechanism is welcome, but NAME every departure, improvements included"* (a gate handed one deviation that finds two should assume a third)
- Reporting law: "report no figure you did not obtain by running a command; state coverage as a limit (read in full / grepped only / not evaluated)"

**1. Scope each session up front**
- Run each agent session's processes in its own cgroup (e.g. a systemd transient scope/unit, `systemd-run --scope`, or a cgroup v2 directory per session) and/or its own session (`setsid`) so it has a process group.

Why is having multiple concurrent agent sessions write to the same git working directory problematic?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"A git working directory is one shared, mutable state, and git is a single-writer tool with no multi-writer protocol — so concurrent agent sessions clobber each other in several concrete ways:

1. **Lost updates at the file level.** Two sessions writing the same file: the last write silently wins. And since agents work read-modify-write, session B can read a file, have A edit it, then write B's stale copy back — A's change vanishes with no signal.
2. **Races on shared `.git/` state.** The index, `HEAD`, branch refs and `index.lock` are shared files. Concurrent `git add`/`commit`/`checkout`/`rebase` collide: some fail with `unable to write new index file`, and some succeed against state the other session was assuming.
3. **State mutation under a running session.** One agent's `git checkout <branch>`, `git stash`, `git rebase` or `git merge` moves the shared HEAD/branch and touches uncommitted files; one session's `git reset`/`git clean` can delete the other's uncommitted work.
4. **Partial visibility.** An agent reading a file mid-write sees a half-written state and diffs/tests against the wrong content.
5. **No attribution.** Uncommitted changes from two sessions are indistinguishable on disk, so you can't tell which session produced a change — breaking rollback, review and debugging (one session's test failure may be caused by the other's in-flight edits).

The standard fix is isolation, not locking: one checkout per session (e.g. `git worktree add` per thread), so working trees are disjoint and only refs are shared — which git is built to handle.

questions.question: When should code changes be committed during multi-step development?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Commit at the end of each step — when the tree is in a coherent, passing state — and one commit per step.

- **Commit when the step is complete and the tree checks out.** For Nix work, that means the flake still evaluates: run `nix flake check --no-build` (or re-evaluate the attribute you touched) and confirm it's clean before committing. A commit that breaks eval is a bad bisection point.
- **Don't commit mid-refactor states.** If a step needs several edits before anything works, keep them uncommitted until the step is done, then commit once it passes.
- **Don't bundle several steps into one commit.** Granular commits let you revert one bad step, bisect a regression to the step that introduced it, and review one logical change at a time.
- **Commit before moving on**, not at the very end. If you stop after step 3 of 5, steps 1–3 are safe and the half-done step 4 is easy to discard.

questions.question: What does a search or census returning zero results prove when verifying an absence claim?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"A search or census returning zero results proves only absence **within the search you actually ran** — not the absence claim itself. Zero hits mean "nothing matching your query was found in the space you covered," which is a lower bound on the evidence, not a proof.

To turn zero results into a valid absence claim, you have to establish the search was *complete*, which fails in several distinct ways:

1. **Scope**: the census covered a subset (one branch, one rev, one directory, one registry). Zero there says nothing about the rest.
2. **Query mismatch**: the thing exists under a different name, spelling, or case; the pattern didn't match it.
3. **Visibility**: the search tool skipped the thing by design — e.g. `grep`/`find` respecting `.gitignore`, hidden files, or permissions — so it was invisible, not absent.
4. **Staleness**: the index or checkout is not the current state, so a newer addition isn't there.
5. **Silent failure**: the search reported zero because it errored partway and was treated as empty.

So what zero results legitimately support is: "no instance of X was found in Y, using method Z, at time T" — and the absence claim is only as strong as the completeness argument you can add on top of that. If the question is "does X exist?", the honest answer is "I did not find X in Y," not "X does not exist."","confidence":0.8,"gaps":["No matching prior answer in the support or memory banks; answered from general reasoning, not from a checked source"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

**Why it hurts:**

1. **It hides typos and renames.** `cfg.paths` misspelled as `cfg.path`: a plain lookup fails with `attribute 'paths' missing` plus a file/line trace; `cfg.path or []` evaluates to `[]` and the typo survives the whole eval. questions.question: Why might bash arrays and word splitting behave differently when running commands in zsh?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because zsh's native expansion rules are intentionally different from bash's, and the bash-like behavior is opt-in: the `zsh(1)` man page (COMPATIBILITY, zsh 5.9) lists that when zsh is invoked as `sh`/`ksh` it enables `SH_WORD_SPLIT`, `KSH_ARRAYS`, and `GLOB_SUBST`. 1. **Word splitting**: `SH_WORD_SPLIT` (set by default only in ksh/sh emulation) "causes field splitting to be performed on unquoted parameter expansions." In bash `cmd $var` splits `$var` on IFS; in native zsh it stays a single word.
2. **Arrays**: `KSH_ARRAYS` (same `<K> <S>` default) makes arrays 0-indexed and makes a bare array name refer to the *first* element. questions.question: Why is checking $? after a piped shell command risky for verifying command success?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because in a pipeline, `$?` only carries the exit status of the **last** command in it. POSIX defines a pipeline's exit status as the exit status of its final command, so every earlier stage is invisible to your check.

The failure mode this creates:

```sh
grep pattern file | sort > out.txt
[ $? -eq 0 ] && echo "success"
```

If `grep` matches nothing (exit 1), `sort` happily succeeds on empty input (exit 0), and `$?` is 0 — so the check reports success even though the data source failed. The same blind spot applies to `set -e` (errexit): it only reacts to the pipeline's final status, not to failures in the earlier stages.

Ways to make the check safe:

1. **`set -o pipefail`** (bash, zsh, ksh93): the pipeline then returns the rightmost non-zero exit status, so any stage's failure propagates into `$?`. Note this is *not* POSIX — plain `sh`/dash don't have it.
2. **Inspect each stage's status**: bash keeps them in the array `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` (e.g. check that every element is 0). Check it immediately, before anything else overwrites it.
3. **Restructure**: run the stages as separate commands and check each one, or write intermediates to a variable/file and test each step.

General hygiene: read `$?` (or `$PIPESTATUS`) right after the pipeline; any intervening command — an assignment, a test, a function call — clobbers it.

How I know: this is standard POSIX shell behavior (pipeline exit status = last command; errexit only sees that same status) and bash's documented `pipefail`/`PIPESTATUS` semantics. questions.question: What happens when using cat file | sed ... > file to transform a file in place?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**The file ends up empty — the original content is lost.** This is not in-place editing; it's the classic data-loss trap of redirecting output to the file you're reading.

**Why.** The shell sets up the `> file` redirection *before* the commands in the pipeline start running. `>` opens the file with truncate-to-zero-size semantics (bash(1), REDIRECTION: *"if it does exist it is truncated to zero size"*; redirections are performed *"before a command is executed"*). So by the time `cat file` runs, `file` is already 0 bytes: `cat` reads an empty file, produces no output, `sed` gets no input and writes nothing, and the final `file` is empty. There is a tiny race (cat opens the file while sed's redirection truncates it), but the truncation reliably wins in practice.

**How to actually transform a file in place:**
- `sed -i 's/old/new/' file` — sed works on a temporary file and renames it over the original, so the input is never truncated first (GNU/BSD sed; not in POSIX sed).

- `perl -pi -e 's/old/new/' file`

**After the write — check whether the written record's hash moved.**

If the new record hashes equal to the old one, the append was a no-op: propagation stops there, and the node keeps its prior trace entry byte-identical. questions.question: When facing a difficult architectural fix, why should an agent avoid settling for a temporary workaround?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short answer: a "temporary" workaround has no owner, no deadline, and no ticket — so it rarely behaves like a temporary thing.

Why an agent should not settle for one when a hard architectural fix is in front of it:

1. **The workaround becomes load-bearing.** Every "just for now" shim gets code built on top of it. After a few weeks, removing it costs more than the original fix would have, and the agent that applied it (or its notes) are long gone. "Temporarily" is the most common prefix on the oldest code in any repo.

2. **It hides the root cause.** A workaround suppresses the symptom; the underlying structural problem stays in place and resurfaces in a new shape. The next diagnosis starts from a muddier baseline, and each successive workaround adds another layer of indirection.

3. **The cost is deferred, not avoided.** The work of doing the architectural fix properly is front-loaded. The workaround pushes that bill into the future with interest: more surface area, more special cases, more context a future reader (or future agent) has to reconstruct from memory of *why* the hack existed.

4. **It narrows future options.** Shims and compat layers lock in interfaces. A workaround chosen today often constrains the shape of the real fix that comes later, because now the fix has to be backward-compatible with the hack.

5. **Silence reads as approval.** If an agent quietly settles, the workaround is implicitly accepted as the design. Nothing flags it for review; nobody questions it; it calcifies.

The nuance: the rule is not "never work around anything." A temporary workaround *can* be the right move when the blast radius is small, it is clearly scoped with an owner and a removal date, and the real architectural fix is actively planned. What an agent should avoid is settling — treating the workaround as the answer, leaving it untracked, and letting it outlive the circumstances that justified it.

**1. One concern per library, loosely coupled.** Each library owns exactly one concern (type checking, module merging, scope-graph evaluation, graph queries, selection, binding, dispatch, dataflow) and names itself after the literature it comes from. They talk to each other through accessor functions and plain attrsets rather than deep coupling, so you can take `gen-graph` without `gen-scope`, or `gen-schema` without knowing what an aspect is.

**2. A pure composition plane with nixpkgs isolated at the terminals.** The substrate (`gen-types → gen-merge → {gen-schema, gen-aspects}`) resolves gen module trees to values without ever touching `lib.evalModules`, and every roster library is nixpkgs-lib-free (enforced per repo by a source scanner). **3. Generic substrate, den as the primary consumer.** None of the libraries knows what NixOS is; the primary consumer is `den` (a NixOS / nix-darwin / home-manager configuration framework). questions.question: An orchestrator is planning their workflow for a session. Should they write implementation code directly in the main session or delegate execution to subagents?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Delegate execution (and review) to fresh-context subagents; keep only judgement.**

The standing rules are explicit: "You keep JUDGEMENT. You hand off EXECUTION and REVIEW to fresh-context subagents" (`orchestrator-operating-rules.md`), and "These rules outrank convenience, precedent and effort estimates."

Key points:

- **Even mechanical (M-tier) work stays delegated.** A mechanical change drops the spec and the gate, but it does *not* drop the delegation — "ceremony and authorship are different axes." The tell that you've slipped: you're hand-writing the third `sed` of a sweep.
- **The orchestrator's turns go to:** adjudicating forks, synthesising verdicts, owner-in-the-loop decisions, and tracker reconciliation. The tracker is the orchestrator's to write; a subagent's findings return to it.
- **Why:** the orchestrator is the scarce, long-lived context. Every plan or spec written inline burns tokens needed to hold the whole arc; workers are cheap and disposable, and their context resets (`delegate-authoring.md`). The owner flagged this drift twice in prior sessions — once toward a generic unnamed agent, once toward cutting independent plan review for a small task.
- **If you do write anything inline, keep it small:** "Small tasks may be planned inline. For anything complex, dispatch the author, review its output, and keep only the decision, not the prose."

questions.question: When working in a shared git checkout where another peer agent is actively modifying files, how should changes be committed?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Commit **path-scoped, in one breath**: `git add <your paths>` then `git commit -m … -- <your paths>`, and verify by accounting, not by exit code.

The full discipline, from the operating memory (`one-writer-per-checkout`, `shared-checkout-peer-sessions`, `peer-sessions` — all measured incidents):

1. **Always `-- <paths>` on the commit.** A bare `git commit` takes the whole shared index and has swept a peer's staged work (once: a 229-line file) into a push. `--amend` is equally dangerous: it amends *whosever* commit sits at HEAD.
2. **Never `stash`, `pull`/`pull --rebase`, `--autostash`, `checkout --`, `restore`, `reset`, `add -A`, `add .` or directory adds in a shared checkout.** A `git stash` there has taken a peer's in-flight edit out of the tree — it survived only in `stash@{0}`.
3. **One writer per file.** Never edit a file the peer has in flight; send them the measurement instead. Path-scoping does not protect two writers in one file.
4. **Verify by accounting.** Before committing: `git diff --cached --name-only` shows only the paths you named. After: `git show --stat HEAD` matches your message and `git status --porcelain | wc -l` is 0. This matters because `git commit -- <paths>` applies to *tracked* files only — it once exited 0 having committed 3 of 18 files while the message claimed all of them.
5. **Mind the pre-commit hook.** It stashes tracked, unstaged changes across the whole worktree even on a path-scoped commit. After every commit run `git status --short` and confirm no peer file vanished; if one did, stop and tell the peer at once. `--no-verify` needs the owner's say-so.
6. **Pushing takes the whole branch.** You push only when `git status --short` shows nothing but your own paths; usually the peer that owns publication pulls and pushes, and that push publishes your commits too. At close, verify each of your shas reached origin (`git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main`, with one unresolvable sha as the control).
7. **If two writers are working in parallel in one repo, the better shape is one writer per checkout**: each writer gets its own worktree (`git worktree add .worktrees/<task> -b wt/<task> HEAD`) and the orchestrator integrates serially from the main checkout.

questions.question: What should an orchestrator do if multiple subagents complete their dispatches and sit idle while context remains low?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Dispatch — that is the whole point of low context. An idle or shrinking fleet below the context threshold (~75%) is a **dispatch trigger, not a finish**. Concretely:

1. **On every agent return, count and refill in the same turn.** Count live agents against the concurrency cap (measured in strong-model equivalents: one strong-tier agent = two mid-tier; e.g. a budget of 6 means 6 strong, or 4 strong + 4 mid, …), and fill **every free slot from the whole ready frontier** — not just the successor of the agent that just returned. Refilling one slot per return is the measured "lane drain" that let a fleet decay from 6 to 2.
2. **Verify "idle" before you treat the slot as free.** "Waiting" is a claim, and idle is not dead: check for a live process (`ps`) and the newest mtime in the agent's scratch dir. No process and stale mtime means stalled — wake it with the completion line from its own output file. If you reassign its repo, stop the old agent first (`TaskStop`), then dispatch the successor; an idle agent still has an inbox and can become a second writer.
3. **Before each dispatch:** confirm the task is actually unblocked and no stalled peer still holds it, name the agent `<task>-<role>`, and pass `model` explicitly (unqualified dispatches silently spend a strong slot). A resume by message also counts as a dispatch for cap purposes.
4. **End the turn on a dispatch** (or on command output proving the queue is empty), not on a summary or a list of questions. A summary is not a deliverable unless asked for.
5. **If you are over the cap, stop dispatching and let it drain — never kill working agents** (killing throws away paid tokens and buys nothing back). Here that case doesn't apply: slots are free.
6. **Keep banking:** owner questions get one tracker row plus one line in the report, then work continues; obligations go into tracker bodies as you go, since a handoff drafted early is wholesale-replaced at close.

questions.question: What essential elements must be provided when writing a dispatch brief for a leaf agent?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"A dispatch brief carries the **task half** of what an agent gets (the agent itself carries the standing half: instrument facts, measurement law, reporting/hand-off protocol). Everything a brief must carry, per the dispatch form and the writing-a-brief practice:

**Identity and tracking**
- **Task id + role** (`scout | spec | gate | build`) — every agent named, visible on the roster
- **Carrier** — the tracker id where findings return
- **Claim** — mark the tracker item `in_progress` *before* sending, release at return; an unclaimed item with an agent on it is a tracker that lies
- **Tier** — `M | D | R`

**What it lands**
- **Target** — the component that lands, plus the demo/corpus example that exercises it (gen-demo for gen) in the same landing
- **Design** — pointer to the owner-approved design, or "existing component"; a brief naming a *new* component without one is not dispatchable
- **Sizing** — lands in one dispatch with its integration arm green, or split before sending

**Tagged premises** (conclusions only, not reasoning)
- `[MEASURED <sha>]` — claim plus the command, so the agent can re-run it
- `[RELAYED <source>]` — who said it; you have not checked it
- `[ASSUMED]` — belief without evidence
- Quote the measured cell and its control, not your compression of a report; a tracker-body citation is `RELAYED`, not `MEASURED`

**Scope**
- **IN** — exactly what to touch; **OUT** — what is excluded, and why that is not an oversight
- **CLASS** — single instance, or discharge the class, with a predicate the agent re-runs; an exemplar is only a mandatory known positive

**Deliverables and worktree**
- A **disk path for every deliverable** (`reports/<task-id>-<subject>-<role>-v0.md`, subject included); check the path is free first — work named only as "report X" gets lost
- A **write / commit / commit+push verb per repo**; fence a repo only where a competing writer exists, never over files the spec lists as outputs
- **Worktree** — `<path>` at an explicit sha (one writer per worktree), or a shared checkout at sha with every read pinned to it

**The oracle**
- **EXIT** — the gating oracle (component landed, consumer builds, example green) and who confirms it, with its RED and GREEN stated; if you cannot state EXIT you do not know what you are asking for
- Specify the **property**, the forbidden shapes, and what a *failing* run looks like — leave the mechanism to the agent unless it is ruled. Include "a better mechanism is welcome, but NAME every departure, improvements included", and "report no figure you did not obtain by running a command; state coverage as a limit (read in full / grepped only / not evaluated)"

**Tells that a brief is wrong before you send it**
- Restates instrument facts the agent already carries (they get restated wrong)
- Says "carefully" or "make sure" — that is not a specification
- Asks for a fix *and* a report in one breath (split: scout, then build)
- Cites "VERIFIED" from a status block — give the sha, let the agent re-derive
- Blends theory, mechanism and argument into one "is this right?" — the three fail independently, ask apart

How I know: read `/memory/workflow/dispatch-form.md` (the template: identity, tier, target, design, sizing, premises, scope, deliverable, worktree, exit) and `/memory/practices/writing-a-dispatch-brief.md` (property + oracle + failure shape, named departures, per-repo verbs, predicate-named classes, disk paths for every deliverable).","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["Answer derived entirely from the memory bank; no eval run (none needed for a practice question)"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: How should long-running or background processes be terminated safely when multiple agent sessions share a machine?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The short version: **only ever kill a PID you captured yourself at launch, with `$!`** — and on a shared machine, make sure nothing you can't kill by PID gets to blow up in the first place.

## Termination rules

1. **Never use `pkill`, `pkill -f`, `killall`, or `kill` on `pgrep -f` output.** `-f` matches the full command line, and the command line that names the pattern contains the pattern — so the kill loop matches the very shell (or its parent) running it. Measured incident: an agent stopped its own probe lanes with `pkill -f '<dir>/run.sh'`, then looped `kill $ppid $pid` over `pgrep -f` output; the pattern matched the shell running that command line, the loop killed the **orchestrator session**, and every live agent had to be resumed by raw id. Two other agents self-matched the same day.
2. **Launch/stop/wait as a pair:** `cmd & pid=$!` → `kill "$pid"` → `wait "$pid"` (or `timeout 3600 zsh -c "while kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null; do sleep 10; done"`). Never loop on `pgrep -f` from the waiting shell.
3. **Wait on a marker file the producer itself writes**, always with a timeout: `timeout 3600 zsh -c 'until [ -e out/ALL-DONE ]; do sleep 10; done'`, where the job writes `ALL-DONE` as its last act. A loop that greps for the script name can match its own command line and never exit — one audit found 13 orphaned waiter shells, 6 minutes to 22 hours old, several of them self-matching.
4. **If you must touch a process you did not start** (inherited session, stray waiter): read its predicate against its target first, enumerate PIDs explicitly, and kill by PID. Treat any pattern-kill in an agent report as a near miss to record.

## Ownership on a shared machine

5. **The orchestrator owns every agent it dispatched** until each returns. Before reassigning a repo: `TaskStop` the old agent, *then* dispatch the successor — never two owners of one tree. Don't close a session while dispatched agents are live.
6. **After killing an agent, check `git status --short` and `git diff` before dispatching a replacement** — the killed agent may leave a half-finished tree; the successor gets an adopt-or-reset choice.

## Cap the things you might not get to kill

7. **Run every eval/build/test under a memory cap**: `systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=12G -p MemorySwapMax=0 --quiet <nix command>`. On a shared machine a runaway job is a shared-machine incident (measured: an agent's test pushed a workstation out of memory and the owner killed it by hand). **rc 137 under the cap is a finding, not an obstacle** — report the command and the cap; never re-run uncapped "to see if it passes". Read the exit status unpiped (`cmd > out 2> err; echo $?`), because a pipe masks the 137.
8. **Don't stack watchers:** subagents poll their own background runs (they don't reliably receive completion notices — measured: agents idling 48 min to 4 h after their runs finished); the orchestrator waits on `run_in_background`'s own notice and arms at most one Monitor, and only for a condition no task signals.
9. **Shell caveat:** the harness runs zsh, not bash. Write loops for zsh (or use `bash -c`), quote expansions, never name a loop variable `path` or `status`, and re-check output after any new loop — several zsh forms fail silently.

**Basis:** `/memory/practices/kill-only-captured-pids.md` (the core rule and incidents), `/memory/practices/agent-liveness-and-ownership.md` (ownership), `/memory/practices/cap-every-heavy-evaluation.md` (caps and rc 137), `/memory/traps/zsh-is-not-bash.md` (shell idioms).

**1. Commands are scoped to the index, the branch, or the whole tree — not to your task.**
- `git commit` takes the *whole index*. A bare commit swept another agent's staged 229-line file into a push. `--amend` amends *whoever's* commit sits at HEAD — one agent destroyed another's commit message that way.
- A push takes the *whole branch*: two path-scoped writers, and one push carried the other's un-gated commits to the public remote as ancestors.
- The index is shared: files left staged across a tool call get swept into the other writer's bare commit.
- Even the scoped form bites: `git commit -- <paths>` applies to **tracked** files only. Without a prior `git add` it exited 0 having committed 3 of 18 files, with a message claiming all of them.

**2. Working-tree operations are global, so one session's housekeeping eats the other's live work.**
- A pre-commit hook stashes tracked, unstaged changes across the *whole worktree*, however the commit is scoped — a concurrent writer's tracked edits vanish during the hook run.
- `git checkout -- .` reverted a peer's uncommitted work and voided its test runs: "green figures for a tree that never held the change." A `git stash` took a peer's in-flight spec edit out of the tree; the edit survived only in `stash@{0}`.
- Read-then-write of a whole file destroyed a peer's edit landed in between. Hence the rule is one writer per **file**, not just per path.

**3. You end up measuring and reporting revisions that don't exist.**
- Clean `git status` is *not* unmoved: a peer landed one commit (+110/−3) in the exact file under review, and porcelain read clean in both states.
- Torn captures: a spec committed while its author still edited — 392 lines against 481 on disk, staged cleanly, read as complete. A diffstat read mid-write matched neither commit that resulted.

**4. History gets entangled and commits become unattributable.**
- Every session commits as the same git user, and `ListAgents` lists only *live* sessions: one session found two unpushed commits, asked all live peers, got "not mine" from each — both were its own immediately-prior context window, ended 44 seconds earlier.
- Two doc agents plus the orchestrator on one repo produced divergent sibling commits; `origin/main` looked clobbered until a rebase recovered it.

**The rule we run:** one writer per checkout, counted per *repo* (two writers on disjoint files still share the index and HEAD). Parallel writers each get `git worktree add .worktrees/<task> -b wt/<task> HEAD` and the orchestrator integrates serially from the main checkout. Where a checkout is genuinely shared: `git add <paths>` then `git commit -m … -- <paths>` in one breath, line-scoped edits only, never `stash`/`pull`/`rebase`/`autostash`/`push`/`checkout --` there — and verify commits by accounting (`git diff --cached --name-only` before, `git show --stat HEAD` after), not by exit code.","confidence":0.9,"gaps":[],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: When should code changes be committed during multi-step development?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Commit after each verified logical unit — not at the end of a session, and not mid-unit.**

The rule, from the operating memory:

1. **Unit → commit → land, in the same dispatch.** Commit once the unit's gate is met; land a gate-passed unit on the repo's `main` in the same dispatch, by its own build agent. Keep history linear: rebase, not merge commits; revert forward-only, never force-push.
2. **Commits are sync points.** Peer agents review by pulling them, so batching up and committing once at the end stalls the loop. Write messages that stand alone for a peer reader.
3. **Cheap checks per commit; the slow plane once on the final tree.** Run the local gate before every push; don't run an ~11-minute suite after each one-cell commit — run expensive checks once on the final tree and bisect only if they red.
4. **Format before each commit.** Run the repo's own formatter on the files you're committing, after the last edit, against the exact landing revision; don't trust an earlier green.
5. **Exception — generated exports** (e.g. a tracker export): don't commit those often (44 export-only commits once destroyed sha-based tree identity). Batch the export once per session phase.
6. **Multi-writer repos:** one writer per checkout; parallel writers get their own worktrees; in a genuinely shared checkout, sub-agents write files only and the orchestrator is the sole committer, with path-scoped commits.
7. **Don't pre-authorize a push for a requirement the owner hasn't confirmed.** A red main after landing is owned by the author of the red commit: diagnose before reverting, then fix forward or revert forward.

How I know: this is a process question, so no eval was needed — I read the governing memory files: `landing-and-history` (commit/land cadence, export exception), `ci-gate-discipline` (check cadence), `format-before-commit`, `one-writer-per-checkout`, and `handoff-and-close` (close-time commits: commit running agents' results first; path-scoped tracker commit, never `-A`).","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["No eval performed (process question); all claims sourced from memory files read this turn, not from a live repository state"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: What does a search or census returning zero results prove when verifying an absence claim?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"A zero from a search or census proves only that **your instrument printed nothing** — it is a property of the measurement, not of the world. It cannot distinguish "the thing is absent" from a broken instrument, a mismatched predicate, or a too-narrow population, because all three read 0 identically.

**What a bare zero does not rule out** (measured cases from the `controls-for-absence-claims` trap, verified 2026-10-15):
- **Broken instrument**: zsh failed to word-split an unquoted `$list` so grep saw one concatenated path; `git grep -lin` parsed as `--lin` and printed nothing; a "database is busy" read exited rc 2 with clean empty stdout (error on stderr) and every grep — positive control included — read 0 until a later attempt returned 3496 lines; an aborting run destroys the output entirely, so no control can fire.
- **Predicate vs. shape mismatch**: a status-glyph prefix made a start-of-line-anchored `grep -c '^<id>'` read 0 over a full result set; a single-predicate census undercounts a unit with two syntactic shapes.
- **Population mismatch**: a glob for `specs/adr/0031*.md` never matches `specs/adr/ledger/0031-*.md`, so the search was doomed to 0 and even a positive control in the same too-narrow domain passed; a "whole-tree => 0" claim was "controlled" by figures taken over `lib/` only.
- **Unarmed comparisons**: a sweep for pattern P "controlled" by pattern Q firing 5 times proves nothing about P; a comparator can be dead while both subjects look fine (a nonexistent arm must report UNUSABLE, never IDENTICAL).
- **Reused negative tokens**: a banked token fires on an earlier run's record and looks like a broken instrument (or a genuine hit gets dismissed as "just a token").

**What makes a zero mean absence:**
1. A **positive control** — same instrument, same flags, same run, on a case *known to match* in the *same population* the claim covers; subject and control in the same command, both values printed. If the control reads 0 too, the instrument is broken: fix it before reporting anything.
2. If the corpus holds no known positive, **plant one and say it was planted**.
3. A **fresh random negative token each run**, never committed.
4. **Read exit status unpiped and check stderr**; on an empty read from a shared store, retry a few times with a short wait before accepting the empty.
5. **Report counts per term including zeros**, and make the sweep refuse (exit 1) when every term is zero.
6. Let the **figure and its population travel together** as one token: `link 7 (lib/ only)`, never bare `link 7`.

So the zero is the null result of your instrument; the absence claim stands only when your control fires.","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["The two supporting files cited beyond controls-for-absence-claims (control-population-must-match-claim, census-predicate-spans-shapes) are marked 'unverified' in the memory index; their measured cases are restated, not independently re-measured here"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

- **Predicate vs. shape mismatch**: a status-glyph prefix made a start-of-line-anchored `grep -c '^<id>'` read 0 over a full result set; a single-predicate census undercounts a unit with two syntactic shapes.
- **Population mismatch**: a glob for `specs/adr/0031*.md` never matches `specs/adr/ledger/0031-*.md`, so the search was doomed to 0 and even a positive control in the same too-narrow domain passed; a "whole-tree => 0" claim was "controlled" by figures taken over `lib/` only.

questions.question: What must exist before a spec or plan can be submitted to a review gate?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**An executable oracle — something runnable that settles the verdict — must exist before a spec, design, or plan is opened to an adversarial review gate. "No oracle, no gate."**

From `/memory/practices/gates-need-an-oracle.md` (the rule):

- Before a gate, **name what settles it**. A test, a differential, or a set of oracle cells that can be run supports review rounds.
- A **person's judgement is not an oracle**: it gets exactly ONE reading by that person, not rounds. Prose always admits another reading, so "run until dry" never terminates on prose — that's why gates need something executable.
- Each oracle cell's **RED and GREEN values must be EVALUATED (actually run) before the cell is written**, not derived from reading the source. A derived expectation inherited from the dispatcher is still derived — an incident caught three stated values false and one control unable to discriminate.

The gate role (`/memory/workflow/roles/gate.md`) matches this: default posture REJECT, and every finding must be a FAIL-IF predicate pointing at a concrete artefact — the oracle is what makes each finding checkable rather than arguable. Relatedly, the practice suggests splitting a large spec into a small frozen core (what the gate attacks) plus a measurement ledger (verified by re-running commands, not re-reading).

So the short answer: a runnable oracle that settles the verdict, with its red/green values already executed. questions.question: What are the decision classification tiers used when filing tasks and architecture decisions?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The tiers are the **M / D / R / N** classes, classified when a change is filed, with the class and a one-line reason written in the tracker body (source: `/memory/practices/decision-tiers.md`):

- **M — mechanical:** the outcome is fully determined by an existing ruling or spec, and a failure would be loud. The tracker body IS the spec (problem, mechanism, oracle); execute directly with its own test, no gate round.
- **D — design:** creates or changes a construct, representation, or public surface. Needs a lean spec, an adversarial gate, and an owner fork where one exists. **A change whose tier is unclear is D** — that is the default.
- **R — ruling-only:** the owner is the oracle. One reading, no manufactured measurement.
- **N — new named thing:** a library, repository, roster member, user-facing surface, or framework component. Starts with a brainstorming session with the owner; a spec is dispatched only against the design that session approved.

Operational rules that come with them:

- An M task that hits an undecided design fork mid-execution **stops and promotes itself** (to D).
- The tell that an N brainstorm was skipped: a spec whose open question is what the thing *is*, *where it lives*, or *what it's called*. Stop and hold the build.
- A D agent revising an owner-approved design does not reword approved sentences — the dispatch asks for a sentence-level diff against the approval revision.
- The M tier removes the spec and the gate, not delegation.

Origin, per the record: the owner's complaint that "the overhead of ceremony has become a risk unto itself" — the N class specifically came from two same-day misses where a new thing fell into D and a spec was dispatched before the owner had been asked.","confidence":0.95,"gaps":[],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: Why are silent fallbacks such as or [] considered harmful when looking up required attributes?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"A missing **required** attribute is a broken contract, and `or []` converts a contract violation into a perfectly plausible value. That is the whole harm: the failure stops happening where it occurred and reappears later, downstream, in a shape that doesn't point at the cause. Concretely:

1. **The refusal is replaced by a value.** `x or []` evaluates to `[]`, a legal value. Downstream code (selection predicates, `head`, filters, provenance logic) consumes it happily, so nothing at the lookup site signals that the contract was broken.
2. **The failure moves and multiplies.** Where it resurfaces depends on which consumers force the value and in what shape — not on where the bug is. Measured incidents from operating memory:
   - One dropped override → the lookup took a warn-path to an **empty** value → evaluation died far downstream on an unrelated assertion. Reported blast radius: **42 cells**; with the lookup pointed at the right field (one line), the real cost was **3 cells, one assertion, zero hard errors**.
   - A field rename hit four consumer sites. One read it bare and **aborted loudly**. Three read it through `or []` and kept "working" with an empty chain: a selection predicate that always held and a provenance hierarchy that silently flattened. **The crash was the cheap half.**
   - A dispatch guard keyed on a destructured argument name silently never fired when the stale name was out of scope. No error; an entire downstream configuration came out empty.
3. **Warnings ride on thunks nobody forces.** `warn "..." (x or [])` is a warn-and-continue: the warning only prints if someone forces the value, and by then the location and cause are gone. So review treats warn-and-return-empty as a finding.
4. **They survive the changes that should kill them.** A hard read fails in CI after a rename or contract change; an `or` default ships. After any rename, the sites that did *not* break are the ones to audit.

**Where fallbacks are right:** where absence is *legitimate*. Where both apply, the convention is to put the fallback at exactly one place — the ingestion boundary — and refuse by name everywhere else. That's what gen-prelude's door construct is for: `checkRequired door names record` checks an open record (missing refused, extras admitted) at the point of use, and every refusal is a catchable, named throw of the form `<door>: ... (in prelude.<construct>)` — localized to the lookup, and it names the missing attribute.

questions.question: How should container images be referenced in deployment manifests and configurations?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Reference container images by digest, not by inline tag.** In Nix-managed deployment manifests and configs, the image field resolves through the repo's tracked image-metadata files and a digest accessor, rendering `repository@sha256:<digest>` with no tag.

Per the recorded practice (`/memory/practices/pin-container-images-by-digest.md`):

- **One metadata file per image** (name, tag, digest, hash, arch, os), at a path keyed `<ns>/<name>`.
- The manifest reads `image = { inherit (images."<ns>/<name>") repository digest; }` → renders `repository@sha256:...`.
- **The updater tool re-resolves digests**: a human bumps the tag in the metadata file, the tool writes the new digest. This makes even rolling tags (e.g. `develop`) safe, because the digest pins exactly what gets pulled.
- **Why:** an inline tag can name an image that does not exist — a deploy broke with `ImagePullBackOff` because a GitHub *release* tag had no matching *container* tag (the registry only published a rolling `develop` tag).
- **Recorded gotchas:**
  - Single-segment official images (`alpine`) break the two-level `<ns>/<name>` layout — use `library/<name>`.
  - Check the updater's output path: one `init` wrote a three-level path (including the registry) that broke the two-level fold into accessor keys. Move the file, then verify the accessor resolves with `nix eval`.
  - Validate a rolling tag exists cheaply before the heavy init: `skopeo inspect docker://<ref>`.

questions.question: Why is checking $? after a piped shell command risky for verifying command success?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer:** in `a | b | c`, `$?` is only the exit status of `c`. Anything earlier in the pipeline can fail while `$?` still reads 0, so a piped chain can report success when only the last stage actually ran.

The failure modes (all measured in our trap memory):

- **Failing producer, silent consumer:** a failing `nix-instantiate` piped into a filter reads as clean success; four tracker `create` calls piped through `grep 'Created'` matched nothing, printed nothing, and all four records were silently never created.

- **`&&` chains read skipped as passed:** `check1 && check2 && check3` where a check is `grep -c` stops at the first grep that exits 1 on no match — the "0" that was the answer you wanted — and every skipped assertion after it reads as passed.
- **Shell spelling trap:** the per-stage array is `$PIPESTATUS` in bash, `$pipestatus` in zsh. The bash spelling under zsh is silently empty, so every exit check looks clean. (Also `cmd 2>&1 | wc -l` can count stderr warnings as matches, turning a true 0 into a 2.)

**Fix — read the status unpiped:** `cmd > out 2> err; rc=$?; echo "rc=$rc"`, then inspect `out` and `err`. Keep stderr visible; the error text is part of the measurement. questions.question: What happens when using cat file | sed ... > file to transform a file in place?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The file ends up **empty** — the original content is lost.

**Why:** the shell sets up all redirections for a pipeline *before* it runs any part of it. So `> file` truncates the file to zero bytes first, and only then does `cat file` start reading — reading a file that's already empty. `sed` then transforms an empty input and writes nothing back. No error is printed; you just lose the file.

**How I know:** no shell in my sandbox, so I didn't re-run the idiom itself, but the operating memory trap `/memory/traps/redirect-truncates-before-read.md` (verified 2026-10-15 on zsh 5.9.2) records exactly this rule — "`>` truncates the file before the command runs" — including a near-miss where truncation-before-read quietly shrank a 38 KB record to 4 KB.

**Fixes, in order of preference:**

1. **`sed -i 's/.../.../' file`** — GNU sed's in-place flag (temp file + rename). On macOS/BSD sed it's `sed -i '' 's/.../.../' file` (the `''` is a mandatory empty suffix).
2. **Temp file + move:** `sed 's/.../.../' file > tmp && mv tmp file` — safe because the redirect targets `tmp`, not the source.

questions.question: Why might newly created files fail to be evaluated by a Nix flake command?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**The usual reason: the flake's source is a git-filtered copy of your tree, and a newly created file that isn't `git add`ed simply isn't in that copy.**

How it works, from nix 2.34.8 source (`src/libfetchers/git.cc`):

- When your flake (or any input) is a **git-typed reference** — `git+file://`, `git+https://`, a GitHub ref, a bare repo, or a local dir that nix resolves as `git+file://` (a stray `.git` in the tree does this) — the source tree is built from the **git index**, not the directory. The fetcher's own `url` docstring says it plainly:
  > "If the URL points to a local directory, and no `ref` or `rev` is given, Nix only considers files added to the Git index, as listed by `git ls-files` but uses the *current file contents* of the Git working directory."
- So an untracked file is silently absent. If `flake.nix` (or any imported expression) references it, the accessor throws (`makeNotAllowedError` in `git.cc`):
  > "Path '…' in the repository '…' is not tracked by Git. To make it visible to Nix, run: `git -C … add '…'`"
  If nothing references it, the evaluation just proceeds without it — a warm, unchanged result. This is a measured incident in our operating memory (verified 2026-10-15 on Nix 2.34.8 / Determinate Nix 3.23.1 / Lix 2.95.3): a planted failing *untracked* file was invisible and the suite went green.
- With `?rev=` (or a rev from the lock file) it's stricter: `getAccessorFromCommit` checks out the **commit tree from git objects** and never consults the working directory at all; a dirty tree is rejected with `Git tree '…' is dirty` unless `--allow-dirty`.

**The fix:** `git add` the new file before running the flake command. A commit is *not* required — the workdir accessor uses the current file contents for index-listed files, the file just has to be in the index.

- **Eval cache** — `nix eval`/`nix flake` uses the eval cache when `use-eval-cache` + pure eval are on, keyed by the flake fingerprint (locked ref + lock file; `openEvalCache`/`getFingerprint` in `flake.cc`). questions.question: When appending a block to a record in a store whose write replaces the whole record, what must you check before and after the write?

{"answer":"A store whose write replaces a whole record makes every append a **read-modify-write**, and the checks are:

**Before the write**
- Check the read's **exit status** (unpiped — a pipeline's exit code is the last command's, and says nothing about whether the first stage produced output) and that its **output is non-empty** before appending.
- The read is **non-deterministic under load**: a 454-line record once returned the literal one-line string `null` (an accessor over an empty result); the read seconds later returned all 454 lines. **Read twice and refuse** if either read is empty, `null`, or the two reads differ. Don't refuse on a fixed minimum length — short records are legitimate.
- Gate the whole-record replacement on the intermediate being non-empty: `test -s body.md || { echo ABORT; exit 1; }`. Measured failure: `>` truncates *before* the read runs, so a failed read left an empty file, the append left only the new block, and the write would have replaced a 38 KB record with 4 KB.

**After the write**
- Verify by **checksum of the preserved prefix** (`head -n <old line count> | md5sum`), never by line count: a truncated record plus a long block can have *more* lines than before.
- **Read back** and require byte-identity with what you wrote.
- If the store's own length guard refuses the write, that is a **measurement that your read was short**: re-read. Never answer it with a force flag — that turns a bad read into a lost record.

questions.question: What is the architectural purpose of the gen library ecosystem?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**gen is an ecosystem of small, independently versioned, pure-Nix libraries for building demand-driven, graph-structured configuration frameworks.** Its architectural purpose, as stated in the ecosystem overview (`/memory/gen/overview.md`), is to reach a *pure graph-based configuration framework*: every aspect is a node, every system and user is an entity node, every relation is an edge that can be queried, and policies are logic programs producing dynamic edges on one execution layer. A concrete configuration framework — den, for NixOS / nix-darwin / home-manager — is then built **on top**. No gen library knows what NixOS is.

The architecture rests on five properties:

1. **One concern per library.** Each member owns exactly one thing, is named after the literature it comes from, ships its own test suite and CI gate, and talks to siblings only through accessor functions and plain attrsets. You take only what you need — `inputs.gen-graph.lib` works without the hub. The hub itself owns no concern; it just publishes the roster (`mkGenLibs`), the four stratum buckets, and flake-modules (per `/memory/gen/gen.md`).
2. **Strict layering.** Four strata ordered `substrate < modules < aspects < framework`; a dependency edge may only point down, and the hub's CI (`direction-of-dependence.nix`) refuses an upward edge by name. The `strata` declaration is total and explicit — a member with no entry is a build error, never a default bucket. The graph is acyclic and shallow (e.g. `prelude`, `algebra`, `select` have zero inputs; `scope`, `graph`, `bind`, `dispatch`, `product` depend on `prelude` only).
3. **Two planes, one crossing.** The composition plane is pure and nixpkgs-free (a per-repo purity scanner refuses nixpkgs); the terminal plane is nixpkgs (gen-delivery's `realize` hands content to per-class terminals). Gen types never leave pure eval — only values cross, so a gen type may ride along as inert data, never into the consumer's options tree.
4. **Conventions that keep the pieces independent.** One concern → one `lib`, and each library self-wires its dependencies so consumers wire nothing. Libraries never reach through a sibling; graphs arrive as accessors (functions), never materialized maps; actions are opaque (libraries provide machinery, consumers provide meaning); and constructs that can't do their job throw a *named refusal* rather than substituting a silent default.
5. **Reference-grade discipline.** Deleting an export needs a domain argument, names answer to the literature (with provenance tracked in the hub's `TERMINOLOGY.md`), and every oracle runs under three evaluators (Nix, Determinate Nix, Lix) in CI.

So in one sentence: gen decomposes "a configuration framework" into single-concern pure-Nix libraries with a strictly downward layering, so a demand-driven graph framework (and den on top of it) is composable from parts that each stay independently testable, pure, and NixOS-agnostic.

questions.question: An orchestrator is planning their workflow for a session. Should they write implementation code directly in the main session or delegate execution to subagents?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Delegate execution to subagents. The orchestrator keeps judgement, and hands off both execution AND review.**

Concretely:

- **Implementation code goes to fresh-context agents** (roles like scout / spec / gate / build). Same for specs, plans and documents. The orchestrator's own turns go to adjudicating forks, synthesising verdicts, owner-in-the-loop decisions, and tracker reconciliation.
- **Why:** the orchestrator is the scarce, long-lived context. Every line of code or plan written inline burns tokens needed to hold the whole arc of the session; workers are cheap and disposable, and their context resets.
- **Small tasks:** planning may happen inline, and a mechanical (M-tier) change may drop the spec and the gate — but it **never drops the delegation**. Ceremony and authorship are different axes. The tell that you've slipped into implementing: *you're hand-writing the third `sed` of a sweep*. A judgement call that surfaces mid-execution argues for dispatching a review, not for typing the edit yourself.
- **Related guardrails if you're planning the pipeline:** one writer per worktree (read-only agents may run concurrently); an auditor does not fix what it audits; a reviewer gets the artefact plus a rubric, not the author's framing; and repairs go to a separate build dispatch.

How I know: this is the standing operating memory — `practices/delegate-authoring` ("The orchestrator keeps JUDGEMENT and delegates execution AND review") and `workflow/orchestrator-operating-rules` §1 ("Orchestrate, do not implement... A mechanical change drops the spec and the gate. It NEVER drops the delegation"), both recalled and read in full.","confidence":0.9,"gaps":[],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: The orchestrator notices context usage is around 50%, with several pending tasks left in the queue. Is it appropriate to wrap up the session early?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"No — 50% context is not a stopping point, and the pending queue is the opposite of a reason to stop.

Per the operating rules (memory: `do-not-wind-down-early`, `keep-the-fleet-full`):

- **< 75% context → start new work freely.** The only gates are: 75% (no fresh *subjects*, keep finishing open streams), 90% (close out: bank obligations, write the handoff), and weekly quota ≥ 95%. At 50% the gate is "dispatch, don't finish."
- **An idle/shrinking fleet is a dispatch trigger, not a finish.** Several pending tasks in the queue means there is work to send out in the same turn — fill every free slot from the ready frontier.
- **Early stop is unrecoverable; a late stop is recoverable.** Stopping at 50% throws away remaining session capacity. A late stop is handled by compaction + re-boot from the resume prompt and handoff.

This is a measured failure mode, not a preference: a session closed its rows, published, summarised and stopped at **54% context** — the owner had to prod it back to work, spending their attention (the scarcest resource) on a prod instead of a decision. The rules explicitly list "a natural place to summarise" and "everything is committed and published" as *false* stop conditions — clean state is not an empty queue.

So the right move at ~50%: keep the fleet full by dispatching from the pending queue. One caveat: act only on a real context reading, not a self-estimate — past self-estimates read 76–88% against real readings of 48–59%, and each high estimate was acted on by declining to dispatch.","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["The ~50% figure is the orchestrator's own report; I did not independently read the context meter, and the rules require acting on a real reading, not an estimate"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: When working in a shared git checkout where another peer agent is actively modifying files, how should changes be committed?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"In a checkout where another live session is writing, commit **path-scoped and in one breath**:

1. **`git add <paths>` then `git commit -m … -- <paths>`** — only files you own: your reports, probes, tracker exports, plus any file the owner explicitly directed you to edit (and tell the peer session in the same act). The prior `git add` matters: `git commit -- <paths>` alone applies to *tracked* files only — measured case: it exited 0 having committed 3 of 18 files.
2. **Never `git stash`, `pull`, `pull --rebase`, `--autostash`, `restore`, `checkout --` or `push` in that checkout.** Measured: a stash took a peer's in-flight edit out of the tree (it survived only in `stash@{0}`), and a bare commit took the whole index and swept a peer's staged work into a push.
3. **Let the peer who owns publication pull before it pushes.** Same local branch, so that push publishes your commits too. If no peer is running, the rules relax: you may `git pull --ff-only` and push your own path-scoped commits, but only when `git status --short` shows nothing you don't own.
4. **Mind the pre-commit hook**: it stashes tracked, unstaged changes across the whole worktree even for a scoped commit. After every commit run `git status --short` and confirm no peer file vanished; if one did, stop and tell the peer at once. Skipping the hook (`--no-verify`) needs the owner's say-so.
5. **Verify the commit by accounting, not exit code**: `git show --stat HEAD` matches the message, and `git diff --cached --name-only` (before) showed only what you named.
6. **Never edit a file the peer has in flight** — one writer per file. Send it the measurement instead.
7. **Confirm publication at close**, after the peer's next push: `git fetch`, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` for each of your commits (with one deliberately unresolvable sha as the control). Report any commit that didn't reach origin.

How I know: operating-memory practices `workflow/shared-checkout-peer-sessions.md`, `practices/one-writer-per-checkout.md` and `practices/peer-sessions.md`, each rule above backed by a measured incident recorded in them (the stash, the 3-of-18 commit, the whole-index sweep).","confidence":0.95,"gaps":[],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: What is the default review stance for an adversarial gate reviewer evaluating a submitted patch or spec?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The default posture is **REJECT**. An adversarial gate reviewer evaluating a submitted spec, design or landing starts from rejection and admits the artefact only when it can state each hypothesis, point at its discharge, and say what happens when the hypothesis fails.

A few specifics from the role doc (operating memory, `workflow/roles/gate.md`, "Role: gate (adversarial review)"):

- Every finding is a **FAIL-IF predicate naming a concrete artefact** — a check that says what input makes the system do the wrong thing.
- The reviewer **does not edit the artefact** — no edit tool, and the shell is not a substitute. It writes a report and returns a verdict; a reviewer that repairs what it judges destroys its own evidence.
- The verdict is explicit, one of: **CONSTRUCTION-CLEAN**, **ACCEPT-WITH-CONDITIONS** (every violation has a named local edit needing no new position), or **REJECT**. Construction findings (the system does the wrong thing on some input) block; policy findings (a future author would decide wrongly) do not.
- Review order: prior art in the tracker first, then citation accuracy, construction-over-repair preference, totality of invariants, stated cost, scoped universals, and conformance to the project's own patterns.

questions.question: What essential elements must be provided when writing a dispatch brief for a leaf agent?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Per the operating-memory bank (`workflow/dispatch-form.md`, `practices/writing-a-dispatch-brief.md`, `practices/brief-premises-are-hypotheses.md`), a dispatch brief carries the **TASK half** of the work — the agent's role already carries the STANDING half (instrument facts, measurement law, reporting and hand-off protocol). The brief **links, it does not restate**.

## The form (the essential elements)

```
You are <task-id>-<role>.            # name every agent; the roster shows it
Agent: scout | spec | gate | build

CARRIER:  <tracker id>               # findings return here
CLAIM:    mark the item in_progress BEFORE sending; release at return
TIER:     M | D | R
TARGET:   the component this lands, and the demo/corpus example that exercises it
DESIGN:   pointer to the owner-approved design, or "existing component"
SIZING:   lands in one dispatch with its integration arm green, or split before sending

PREMISE - tag every line; conclusions only:
  [MEASURED <sha>]   <claim> -- <the command, so the agent can re-run it>
  [RELAYED <source>] <claim> -- who said it; you have not checked
  [ASSUMED]          <claim> -- belief without evidence

SCOPE:
  IN:     exactly what to touch
  OUT:    what is excluded, and why it is not an oversight
  CLASS:  instance | discharge the class (and how to enumerate members)

DELIVERABLE: reports/<task-id>-<subject>-<role>-v0.md   (check the path is FREE first)
             WRITE | COMMIT | COMMIT+PUSH -- say which, PER REPO
WORKTREE:    <path> at <explicit sha>  -- one writer per worktree
             (or SHARED CHECKOUT at <sha>; pin every read to the sha)
EXIT:        the gating oracle (component landed, consumer builds, example green) and who confirms it
```
